Momentum + Gold, With a Drawdown Catch

50/50 Midcap150 Momentum-10 + gold — but a 20% drawdown in the momentum leg sells all the gold into momentum, held until a full recovery, then reset back to 50/50.

2009-01-02–2026-08-24 · 5 trigger cycles
Report generated 2026-08-24 12:17

The rule, and the honest result up front

● reduces drawdown vs. pure momentum● underperforms just leaving it alone● 5 trigger cycles in 17.6 years

Start 50% Midcap150 Momentum-10 / 50% gold. The moment the momentum leg falls 20% below its OWN running peak, sell 100% of the gold and put it all into momentum — an all-in lump sum funded by the diversification cushion. Stay 100% momentum until it makes a brand-new all-time high (fully recovers), then reset to exactly 50/50 and repeat. This happened 5 times over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, averaging 237 days to recover each time.

The catch does what it's designed to do on the risk side — shallower drawdown than holding pure momentum alone. But on return, it underperforms simply buying 50/50 once and never touching it again (+31.2% CAGR vs. +35.3%) — and it even underperforms a plain CALENDAR-rebalanced 50/50 blend on drawdown (-29.2% vs. -21.7%). Repeatedly resetting back to 50/50 after each recovery turns out to cap the compounding of the far-faster-growing momentum leg more than the "buy the dip" timing helps — see the honesty note below for the mechanism.

Why "buying the dip" here still lost to doing nothing

▲ framing

WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.

Over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, momentum alone compounded at +40.5% a year versus gold's +13.9% — momentum grew roughly 403x versus gold's 9x over the full window. A 50/50 split that is NEVER rebalanced naturally drifts to be almost entirely momentum within a few years, simply because the faster-compounding asset dominates the mix — that drift is exactly what "static, never touched" is capturing, and it's a large share of why it wins.

The catch rule does the opposite at every single cycle: the moment momentum recovers from a dip, it forcibly resets the mix back to 50/50 — selling down exactly the asset that was about to keep compounding fastest, and buying back into gold, right as momentum turns UP again. Each of the 5 reset points is a small, repeated tax on the momentum leg's own compounding, paid in exchange for a real but partial reduction in how deep the worst drawdown gets.

That trade-off shows up exactly as expected: the catch's max drawdown (-29.2%) is shallower than pure momentum's (-35.1%) — the rule does work as risk management. It just isn't a free lunch: plain periodic rebalancing, with no drawdown-timing logic at all, achieves an even shallower drawdown (-21.7%) for a similar return give-up, suggesting the discipline of rebalancing itself — not the specific -20%/new-high timing rule — is doing most of the risk reduction here.

Limitations

▲ read before trusting any number above

WHAT THIS SHOWS — every simplification behind this backtest.

  • Midcap150 Momentum 10 is reused exactly as built in report 16 — today's fixed Midcap 150 constituent list applied retroactively (survivorship bias), equal-weighted top 10, June/December rebalance (borrowed from the NIFTY200 Momentum convention, not the real Midcap150 Momentum index's own May/November cadence).
  • Only ONE drawdown threshold (-20%) and ONE exit condition (a full new all-time high) were tested — a shallower/deeper trigger, or a partial-recovery exit (e.g. "halfway back"), are untested alternatives that could change this result in either direction.
  • Zero transaction costs, slippage, or taxes modeled on any of the reallocation events (5 triggers + 5 resets = 10 trades total) — a much smaller concern here than report 19's sector rotation, given how few trades this rule generates, but still not zero in practice.
  • As of the last data point, the rule is back in its normal 50/50 state (not mid-drawdown) — see the pill above the trigger timeline; this wasn't cherry-picked, it's simply where the 2025-01-28 → 2025-12-23 cycle happened to land relative to today's date.
  • The "periodic 50/50 rebalance" comparison line reuses report 14's exact blending mechanics (backtest13.blend_50_50) but on the Momentum-10 leg instead of report 14's Momentum-20 — it is NOT report 14's own number restated, it's freshly computed here for a fair, matched comparison.
  • Prices are unadjusted; no dividends are modelled for gold, momentum, or NIFTY 50.
  • This is a single, fixed historical path — 5 trigger events is not a large sample to judge a timing rule's reliability by; a different 17.6-year window could show a very different trigger count and outcome.
